title: Why Reform bans journalists like me
gist: Reform UK revoked press accreditation for its 2026 Birmingham conference from journalists (including the author, Michael Crick and the Guardian's Anna Isaac) who had published critical stories on the party's finances, while Farage and lieutenants increasingly bypass press scrutiny via social media and hostile pushback against journalists.

insights.claim: Reform UK revoked conference press passes from journalists who had recently published critical stories about the party, including Peter Geoghegan (after a piece on Isabel Oakeshott), Michael Crick, and the Guardian's Anna Isaac (who broke the Christopher Harborne £5m donation story).
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: A political party willing to selectively exclude critical press ahead of an election is a signal of reduced transparency risk for its backers/donors but heightened governance and reputational risk for investors or partners tied to the party.
insights.quote: Reform revoked my press accreditation for this year's conference, alongside those of other journalists who have written stories critical of Nigel Farage and his party.

insights.claim: When negative stories broke, Farage abandoned his regular weekly press conferences and shifted communication to social media, while also filing an Ofcom complaint against Sky News over coverage of his daughter.
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: A pivot from press conferences to direct social-media messaging reduces the ability of outside observers, including investors, to get unscripted signal on party positioning and donor relationships ahead of the election.
insights.locator: paragraph on Farage stopping press conferences

insights.claim: Reform surrogates have responded to critical investigative reporting by attacking the credibility of the outlets rather than addressing the substance: Robert Jenrick called the Sunday Times a 'Labour paper' after it reported undisclosed funding from convicted fraudster George Cottrell, and Zia Yusuf frames mainstream coverage of himself as a biased 'Tory press' campaign.
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: A pattern of discrediting rather than rebutting scrutiny of party finances is a red flag for anyone assessing the reliability of Reform's public financial disclosures or its donor base.
insights.quote: Robert Jenrick, with a straight face, said that the Murdoch title was a "Labour paper."

insights.claim: Reform deputy leader Richard Tice and his lawyer did not respond to roughly 40 phone calls, emails and texts from Sunday Times Insight editor Gabriel Pogrund seeking comment on Tice's tax affairs, prompting Pogrund to say Reform does not accept the basic premise of scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: Non-response to sustained, serious inquiries about a senior party figure's tax affairs signals elevated legal/regulatory risk around Reform's leadership finances that due diligence should flag.
insights.quote: Reform seems to not "accept the basic premise of scrutiny."

insights.claim: An undercover Channel 4 investigation broadcast in early September 2026 appeared to show senior Reform figures arranging for a US company to fund opinion polling, potentially in breach of UK election law.
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: Allegations of foreign-funded polling for a party currently polling strongly create legal/regulatory tail risk (Electoral Commission action) that could affect Reform's momentum ahead of the next general election.

insights.claim: Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto entrepreneur, gave Farage a £5m 'gift' that is now the subject of a UK parliamentary standards inquiry; journalist Isabel Oakeshott (partner of Richard Tice) had privately called Harborne 'untrustworthy' before the 2024 election yet publicly defended the donation.
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: An active parliamentary standards inquiry into a £5m donation from a crypto-tycoon donor is a concrete governance/regulatory catalyst to monitor for Reform-linked headline risk.

insights.claim: The author argues that excluding critical journalists from party conferences matters beyond individual reporters because conferences are one of the few venues where journalists can access senior politicians directly and pick up unscripted intelligence from rank-and-file members and lobbyists.
insights.speaker: Peter Geoghegan
insights.so_what: Reduced journalist access to a rising party's internal gatherings means slower discovery of governance and financing issues, raising the value of alternative channels (leaks, FOI, parliamentary inquiries) for tracking Reform-related risk.
insights.locator: paragraph on conferences as access points
